title: Netflix Docuseries on Michael Jackson Trial Ignites Subscriber Revolt and Record Viewership
excerpt: Michael Jackson: The Verdict drew 17.8 million views in five days while sparking a massive backlash, with over 160,000 fans signing a petition demanding Netflix pull the series.
body:
• Netflix's three-part docuseries Michael Jackson: The Verdict revisits the singer's 2005 child molestation trial, featuring interviews with jurors, prosecutors and eyewitnesses.
  • The series pulled 17.8 million views and 47 million hours watched in its first five days, outperforming Netflix's previous record holder, the Beckham documentary.
  • A Change.org petition gathered over 160,000 signatures demanding Netflix pull the series, and fans flooded social media with subscription cancellation screenshots.
  • The docuseries arrived weeks after the Michael Jackson biopic grossed over $850 million at the box office, leading critics to accuse Netflix of opportunistic timing.

Netflix's three-part documentary Michael Jackson: The Verdict has become one of the most polarizing releases in the streamer's history, simultaneously shattering viewership records and triggering a subscriber revolt that shows no signs of abating.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=rcp-j0StBR0

The docuseries, directed by Nick Green and produced by Candle True Stories, revisits the 2005 criminal trial in which Jackson faced multiple counts of child molestation. He was acquitted on all charges after a 14-week trial in Santa Barbara Superior Court. The series features new interviews with jurors, prosecutors, defense attorneys, journalists and eyewitnesses who were present in the courtroom.

Record-Breaking Numbers, Record Backlash

In its first five days on the platform, The Verdict pulled 17.8 million views and 47 million hours watched globally, surpassing the Beckham documentary's 12.4 million views at launch to become one of Netflix's most-watched documentary debuts. The series claimed the number one spot on the platform globally.

The viewership, however, came with a fierce backlash. Jackson's supporters launched coordinated campaigns across social media, posting subscription cancellation screenshots and using hashtag campaigns to pressure Netflix. A Change.org petition demanding the series be pulled gathered over 160,000 signatures. The documentary's audience score on Rotten Tomatoes plummeted to 6 percent, even as critics rated it at 78 percent.

Disturbing Revelations and Familiar Controversy

Among the most discussed moments in the series is an interview with former crisis publicist Vincent Amen, who claims Jackson used crude nicknames for boys he interacted with. Amen describes Polaroid photographs of the accuser Gavin Arvizo's family taken at Neverland Ranch, including one with a disturbing handwritten note.

Former prosecutor Ron Zonen offers one of the strongest statements in the series, maintaining his belief that Jackson was guilty despite the acquittal. On the other side, the defense's perspective is presented through attorneys and associates who argue the accusations were motivated by financial gain.

"It has been 20 years since the trial of Michael Jackson in which he was found not guilty. Yet, to this day, controversy still rages. No cameras were allowed in court, and so the public's view of the facts at the time was filtered by commentators and presented piecemeal."

— Nick Green and Fiona Stourton, filmmakers, via Netflix Tudum

Notably absent from the documentary is Thomas Mesereau, the attorney who secured Jackson's acquittal. Mesereau reportedly refused to participate, calling the case "closed." Family attorney Brian Oxman, who does appear in the series, subsequently called it a "hatchet job."

The Timing Question

The docuseries premiered weeks after Antoine Fuqua's biopic Michael, starring Jackson's nephew Jaafar Jackson, dominated theaters with over $850 million in worldwide gross. The biopic notably avoided the abuse allegations entirely, with its screenplay reportedly gutted of a dramatization of the 1993 lawsuit due to a confidential settlement clause.

Critics accused Netflix of capitalizing on the renewed interest in Jackson's life generated by the biopic's commercial success. Supporters of the series counter that two decades of distance from the trial warranted a thorough re-examination, particularly given that no cameras were allowed in the courtroom during the original proceedings.

Cultural Resonance

Jackson remains one of the most recognized entertainers globally, with a massive following across South Asia. The debate surrounding The Verdict reflects broader tensions between preserving artistic legacies and reckoning with serious allegations — a conversation that extends well beyond Western audiences. Jackson died in June 2009 at age 50. He was never convicted of any crime. His estate continues to deny all allegations of misconduct.
nri_angle: Michael Jackson's enduring popularity in India, where he remains one of the most recognized Western entertainers, makes the documentary's allegations and the surrounding debate a topic of active interest among diaspora audiences.
